cp-2.1.3-prob-quantiles-cs1016.json.title: Exponential claim sizes: CDF and median
cp-2.1.3-prob-quantiles-cs1016.json.problem_statement: Household claim sizes X (£) are modelled as Exponential with mean θ = 800. Compute (a) P(X ≤ 400) and (b) the median claim size.
cp-2.1.3-prob-quantiles-cs1016.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Write the Exponential CDF and survival forms first, then evaluate at 400 and invert for the median.

steps.label: Evaluate the CDF at 400
steps.attempt_cue: Use F(x) = 1 − e^{−x/θ} with x = 400 and θ = 800.
steps.explanation: For an Exponential with mean θ, the CDF is 1 − e^{−x/θ}. The threshold is half the mean, so the exponent is −1/2.

steps.label: Invert for the median
steps.attempt_cue: Solve 1 − e^{−m/800} = 0.5 for m.
steps.explanation: The median is the 0.5-quantile. Survival equals one half when e^{−m/θ} = 1/2, so m = θ ln 2.

steps.label: Refuse recognition-as-evaluation
steps.attempt_cue: State why naming Exponential does not replace the CDF and quantile arithmetic.
steps.explanation: Recognising the family identifies which formulas apply. Probability and quantile questions still require substituting the given numbers into those formulas.
steps.calculation: Family name ≠ numeric F(400) or m_{0.5}

cp-2.1.3-prob-quantiles-cs1016.json.final_answer: P(X ≤ 400) ≈ 0.3935; median ≈ £554.5. Naming Exponential does not replace these calculations.
cp-2.1.3-prob-quantiles-cs1016.json.common_pitfall: Treating P(X ≤ 400) as 0.5 because 400 is half the mean 800, or reporting the median as 0.5 × 800 = 400 instead of θ ln 2.

cp-2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1016.jso.title: Marginal and conditional from a joint claim table
cp-2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1016.jso.problem_statement: A policy year records indicators (X, Y) with joint PMF P(0,0) = 0.05, P(0,1) = 0.15, P(1,0) = 0.20, P(1,1) = 0.60, where X = 1 if a weather claim occurs and Y = 1 if a liability claim occurs. Compute P(X = 1) and P(Y = 0 | X = 1).
cp-2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1016.jso.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Sum the X = 1 column for the marginal, then divide the joint cell by that marginal for the conditional.

steps.label: Form the marginal P(X = 1)
steps.attempt_cue: Add the joint probabilities with X = 1.
steps.explanation: The marginal for X = 1 sums over Y: P(X = 1) = P(1,0) + P(1,1).

steps.label: Form the conditional P(Y = 0 | X = 1)
steps.attempt_cue: Divide P(1,0) by P(X = 1).
steps.explanation: Conditional probability renormalises the joint cell by the matching marginal.

steps.label: Refuse joint-as-marginal
steps.attempt_cue: State why P(1,1) = 0.60 is not P(X = 1).
steps.explanation: A single joint cell is not a marginal. Marginals sum across the other variable; conditionals divide by that sum.

cp-2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1016.jso.final_answer: P(X = 1) = 0.80; P(Y = 0 | X = 1) = 0.25. The joint table is not interchangeable with its margins or conditionals without these moves.
cp-2.2.1-marginal-conditional-cs1016.jso.common_pitfall: Reporting P(X = 1) = 0.60 because P(1,1) is the largest cell, or taking P(Y = 0 | X = 1) = 0.20 without dividing by the marginal 0.80.

cp-2.5.1-clt-cs1016.json.title: CLT probability for a mean repair cost
cp-2.5.1-clt-cs1016.json.problem_statement: Repair costs are iid with mean μ = 1200 and standard deviation σ = 300. A sample of n = 36 repairs is drawn. Using the CLT, approximate P(X̄ < 1150). Use Φ(1) ≈ 0.841.
cp-2.5.1-clt-cs1016.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form the sampling sd σ/√n first, then standardise 1150 before reading Φ.

steps.label: Standard error of the sample mean
steps.attempt_cue: Compute σ/√n.
steps.explanation: Under the CLT for iid observations, X̄ is approximately Normal with mean μ and sd σ/√n.

steps.label: Standardise and evaluate the lower tail
steps.attempt_cue: Form z = (1150 − 1200)/50, then convert with Φ.
steps.explanation: The probability is the lower Normal tail at z = −1, equal to 1 − Φ(1).

steps.label: Refuse σ in place of σ/√n
steps.attempt_cue: State why using sd = 300 for X̄ is wrong.
steps.explanation: The CLT approximates the distribution of the sample mean, whose spread shrinks by √n. Using the population sd as if it were sd(X̄) ignores that reduction.

cp-2.5.1-clt-cs1016.json.final_answer: X̄ ≈ Normal(1200, 50); z = −1; P(X̄ < 1150) ≈ 0.159. Casual Normal use without stating the IID CLT sampling sd is not the same skill.
cp-2.5.1-clt-cs1016.json.common_pitfall: Using X̄ ≈ Normal(1200, 300) and computing z = (1150 − 1200)/300 = −1/6, or reading Φ(1) ≈ 0.841 as the lower-tail probability itself.

cp-2.6.1-random-samples-cs1016.json.title: Classify a convenience extract as not a random sample
cp-2.6.1-random-samples-cs1016.json.problem_statement: An analyst pulls the 40 most recent claims from one large commercial client and treats them as a random sample from the whole motor book in order to build an estimator for portfolio mean severity. Decide whether this extract is a random sample from the stated population, and name the sampling defect.

given.value: 40 most recent claims, one commercial client

cp-2.6.1-random-samples-cs1016.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Compare the selection mechanism with an iid (or otherwise stated) draw from the motor-book population before judging the sample label.

steps.label: State what a random sample requires
steps.attempt_cue: Name the warrant that links observations to the population distribution.
steps.explanation: A random sample is drawn so that observations follow the population distribution under a stated sampling model (for example iid draws). Estimators and intervals inherit that warrant.
steps.calculation: Require: stated sampling model linking extract to motor-book population
steps.result: Random sample = lawful draw under a sampling model

steps.label: Inspect the actual selection mechanism
steps.attempt_cue: Describe how the 40 claims were chosen.
steps.explanation: The extract is consecutive recent claims from one client. That clusters time and client, so dependence and selection bias enter relative to the whole motor book.
steps.calculation: Mechanism = one-client recent slice (clustered, not portfolio iid)
steps.result: Selection is convenience / clustered, not portfolio random

steps.label: Classify and refuse n-as-warrant
steps.attempt_cue: Decide yes/no on random sample, and say why n = 40 alone fails.
steps.explanation: Having forty observations does not create a random sample. Without a lawful draw from the motor book, estimator procedures lack the sampling warrant.
steps.calculation: Classification: NOT a random sample from the motor book; defect = selection bias / clustering
steps.result: Not a random sample; n alone is insufficient

cp-2.6.1-random-samples-cs1016.json.final_answer: Not a random sample from the whole motor book: one-client consecutive claims are clustered and selection-biased. n = 40 does not by itself create a random sample.
cp-2.6.1-random-samples-cs1016.json.common_pitfall: Treating any large enough extract as a random sample because n = 40 looks adequate, without checking whether the draw matches the stated portfolio population.

cp-4.1.1-linear-regression-cs1016.json.title: Assign Y and X, then evaluate a premium line
cp-4.1.1-linear-regression-cs1016.json.problem_statement: A household contents pricing analyst models renewal premium (£). The fitted simple linear relationship from a pilot sample is ŷ = 180 + 12x, where x is sum insured in £000. (a) Name the response and the explanatory variable. (b) Compute the fitted mean premium at sum insured = 25 (£000).
cp-4.1.1-linear-regression-cs1016.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Name Y and X in one sentence, then substitute x = 25 into ŷ.

steps.label: Assign response and explanatory roles
steps.attempt_cue: State which quantity is Y and which is X.
steps.explanation: The modelling question is renewal premium, so premium is the response Y. Sum insured is the predictor used to explain premium, so sum insured is the explanatory variable X.
steps.calculation: Y = renewal premium (£); X = sum insured (£000)

steps.label: Evaluate the fitted mean at x = 25
steps.attempt_cue: Substitute x = 25 into ŷ = 180 + 12x.
steps.explanation: Once roles are fixed, the fitted line gives the modelled mean response at a chosen X value.

steps.label: Refuse column-soup
steps.attempt_cue: State why postcode band is not automatically an X, and why premium is not an X for sum insured.
steps.explanation: Explanatory variables need a modelling warrant for the stated question. Dumping every numeric column on the right-hand side is not role assignment. Treating premium as X for sum insured answers a different modelling question.
steps.calculation: Roles fixed by the modelling question (premium on Y), not by column presence
steps.result: Roles follow the question, not the column list

cp-4.1.1-linear-regression-cs1016.json.final_answer: Y = renewal premium, X = sum insured; ŷ(25) = £480. Postcode band is not automatically explanatory, and premium is not an X for sum insured under this question.
cp-4.1.1-linear-regression-cs1016.json.common_pitfall: Treating every numeric policy field as an explanatory variable for premium, or swapping roles so that sum insured is modelled as Y and premium as X.

cp-5.1.1-bayes-theorem-cs1016.json.title: Bayes update for a cyber-breach alert
cp-5.1.1-bayes-theorem-cs1016.json.problem_statement: In a commercial cyber book, P(Breach) = 0.03. An intrusion-detection rule raises an alert with P(Alert|Breach) = 0.88 and P(Alert|no Breach) = 0.12. A randomly chosen policy raises an alert. Compute P(Alert) and then P(Breach|Alert).
cp-5.1.1-bayes-theorem-cs1016.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Expand P(Alert) by the law of total probability before forming the posterior.

steps.label: Compute the evidence P(Alert)
steps.attempt_cue: Write P(Alert) = P(Alert|Breach)P(Breach) + P(Alert|no Breach)P(no Breach).
steps.explanation: The alert rate mixes true breach alerts and false positives from non-breach policies.

steps.label: Compute the posterior P(Breach|Alert)
steps.attempt_cue: Apply Bayes: P(Breach|Alert) = P(Alert|Breach)P(Breach) / P(Alert).
steps.explanation: Posterior equals prior times likelihood, normalised by the evidence from Step 1.

steps.label: Refuse posterior equals sensitivity
steps.attempt_cue: State why P(Breach|Alert) is not 0.88.
steps.explanation: Sensitivity P(Alert|Breach) is not the posterior. Most alerts still arise from the large non-breach share because the prior breach rate is small.
steps.calculation: 0.88 is P(Alert|Breach), not P(Breach|Alert)

cp-5.1.1-bayes-theorem-cs1016.json.final_answer: P(Alert) = 0.1428; P(Breach|Alert) ≈ 0.1849. Refuse equating P(Breach|Alert) with P(Alert|Breach) = 0.88.
cp-5.1.1-bayes-theorem-cs1016.json.common_pitfall: Setting P(Breach|Alert) = 0.88 (the true-positive rate) and ignoring the base rate and the large false-positive contribution to P(Alert).

cr-1.1.1-aims-analysis-cs1017.json.title: Classify descriptive, inferential, and predictive aims
cr-1.1.1-aims-analysis-cs1017.json.problem_statement: A motor pricing review lists three tasks: (A) draw a histogram of last year's claim severities; (B) form a confidence interval for mean severity; (C) fit a model that forecasts next year's severity. Assign each task to descriptive, inferential, or predictive analysis.

given.value: histogram of last year's claim severities

cr-1.1.1-aims-analysis-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. For each task, ask whether the target is a summary of seen data, a population parameter under uncertainty, or a future value.

steps.label: Classify Task A
steps.attempt_cue: Is A summarising observed data or generalising/forecasting?
steps.explanation: A histogram of last year's severities summarises what was observed. That is a descriptive aim.
steps.calculation: A → descriptive (summarise observed severities)

steps.label: Classify Task B
steps.attempt_cue: What does a CI for mean severity target?
steps.explanation: A confidence interval generalises from sample evidence to a population parameter under uncertainty. That is an inferential aim.
steps.calculation: B → inferential (parameter under uncertainty)

steps.label: Classify Task C and refuse EDA collapse
steps.attempt_cue: Name C's aim, then say why A/B/C are not 'just EDA'.
steps.explanation: Forecasting next year's severity targets a future outcome, so C is predictive. Calling all three 'just EDA' collapses distinct aims.
steps.calculation: C → predictive; refuse A=B=C='EDA'

cr-1.1.1-aims-analysis-cs1017.json.final_answer: A descriptive; B inferential; C predictive. Calling all three 'just EDA' collapses distinct analysis aims.
cr-1.1.1-aims-analysis-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Labelling every pricing-review task as exploratory data analysis, so that confidence intervals and forecasts are treated as the same aim as a histogram.

cr-1.1.2-stages-tools-cs1017.json.title: Order analysis stages and pair an exploratory tool
cr-1.1.2-stages-tools-cs1017.json.problem_statement: You are running a reserves data analysis. State a sensible ordered path of main stages from aim to communication, place exploratory work in that path, and name one suitable tool class for the exploratory stage.
cr-1.1.2-stages-tools-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Sketch the stage sequence first, then locate explore and name a tool class that serves that stage.

steps.label: State the ordered stages
steps.attempt_cue: List aim → data → clean/explore → analyse → communicate.
steps.explanation: A coherent path runs from defining the aim through obtaining data, cleaning and exploring, analysing (infer or predict), then communicating results.
steps.calculation: Order: define aim → obtain data → clean/explore → analyse → communicate

steps.label: Locate exploratory work
steps.attempt_cue: Name which stage holds EDA.
steps.explanation: Exploratory work sits in clean/explore, after data are obtained and before formal inferential or predictive analysis.
steps.calculation: EDA location = clean/explore stage
steps.result: Explore sits after obtain-data, before analyse

steps.label: Pair a tool class and refuse open-notebook-as-done
steps.attempt_cue: Name a tool class for explore, and reject 'opened a notebook' as finishing the path.
steps.explanation: Summary statistics and exploratory visualisations (or data-wrangling scripts) serve clean/explore. Opening a notebook and loading packages does not finish the staged path.
steps.calculation: Tool class for explore: summaries / exploratory plots; notebook-open ≠ path complete

cr-1.1.2-stages-tools-cs1017.json.final_answer: Stages: define aim → obtain data → clean/explore → analyse → communicate. Exploratory work sits in clean/explore and pairs with summary statistics and exploratory visualisations. Opening a notebook does not finish the path.
cr-1.1.2-stages-tools-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Treating 'I opened a notebook and imported packages' as completing analysis staging, without placing exploratory tools inside an ordered aim-to-communicate path.

cr-1.1.3-data-sources-cs1017.json.title: Contrast admin claims extract with a voluntary survey
cr-1.1.3-data-sources-cs1017.json.problem_statement: The same pricing question can be answered from an administrative claims extract or from a voluntary customer survey. Contrast the two sources on bias or coverage, and state why a very large survey sample size does not automatically make the survey the better source.
cr-1.1.3-data-sources-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Compare selection/coverage risks first, then separate volume from representativeness.

steps.label: Contrast bias and coverage
steps.attempt_cue: Name one bias or coverage difference between admin extract and survey.
steps.explanation: Administrative records cover booked claims but may miss unreported events or soft fields. Voluntary surveys often suffer response or selection bias and uneven coverage of the risk population.
steps.calculation: Contrast: admin coverage vs survey response/selection bias (and field completeness)
steps.result: Sources differ in bias and coverage risks

steps.label: Note large-set constraints without equating volume to quality
steps.attempt_cue: State one scale issue and refuse 'larger n ⇒ better data'.
steps.explanation: Extremely large sets can still need sampling or distributed tooling. Large n does not repair non-representativeness by itself.
steps.calculation: Large n ≠ automatic fitness; scale may still require sampling/tooling
steps.result: Volume is not automatically better data

steps.label: Judgment for the pricing question
steps.attempt_cue: State how to choose between A and B for pricing.
steps.explanation: Choose by matching source bias, coverage, and measurement properties to the pricing question, not by raw row count alone.
steps.calculation: Decision rule: fitness = bias/coverage/measurement match, not n-max
steps.result: Prefer source fitness over largest n

cr-1.1.3-data-sources-cs1017.json.final_answer: Admin extract and voluntary survey differ in selection/response bias and coverage. Large survey n does not automatically fix representativeness or make the survey better for the pricing question.
cr-1.1.3-data-sources-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Assuming the voluntary survey is better whenever its row count exceeds the admin extract, without comparing bias, coverage, and measurement quality for the pricing use.

cr-1.1.4-reproducible-cs1017.json.title: Judge whether a one-cell notebook rerun is reproducible
cr-1.1.4-reproducible-cs1017.json.problem_statement: A colleague says their pricing analysis is reproducible because they can re-run one notebook cell on their laptop. Decide whether that claim meets the definition of reproducible research, and name required elements that are still missing.

given.value: re-run one notebook cell on their laptop
others can reconstruct the same results from stated inputs and steps

cr-1.1.4-reproducible-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Compare the colleague's evidence with the reconstruct-from-shared-artefacts standard before judging.

steps.label: State the reproducibility standard
steps.attempt_cue: Define reproducible research in one sentence.
steps.explanation: Reproducible research lets others (or a future you) reconstruct the same analysis results from stated inputs and steps.
steps.calculation: Standard = reconstruct same results from stated inputs/steps

steps.label: List required elements
steps.attempt_cue: Name data, code, and environment/documentation pieces.
steps.explanation: Required elements include versioned or clearly identified data, scripted code paths, and documented environment and decisions (including parameters/seeds where relevant).
steps.calculation: Need: versioned/identified data + scripted code + documented environment/decisions

steps.label: Judge the colleague claim
steps.attempt_cue: Decide pass/fail and name what a one-cell local rerun lacks.
steps.explanation: A one-off local re-run without shared artefacts does not let others reconstruct the analysis. The claim fails the reproducibility standard.
steps.calculation: Judgment: FAIL; missing shared data identity, full scripted path, and environment docs
steps.result: Not reproducible under the reconstruction standard

cr-1.1.4-reproducible-cs1017.json.final_answer: Not reproducible: a one-off local notebook-cell rerun lacks shared versioned data, scripted end-to-end code, and documented environment/decisions that others can use to reconstruct the results.
cr-1.1.4-reproducible-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Equating 'I can re-run this cell on my laptop' with reproducibility, without requiring shared artefacts that let someone else reconstruct the same results.

cr-1.2.1-eda-summaries-cs1017.json.title: Choose summaries for zero-inflated claim counts
cr-1.2.1-eda-summaries-cs1017.json.problem_statement: Five policy-years show claim counts 0, 0, 1, 3, 10 (many zeros and a long right tail). Aim: explore frequency shape before modelling. Compute the mean and median, then choose an exploratory summary/plot approach that reveals zero mass and the tail.

given.note: EDA tool choice, not a full model fit

cr-1.2.1-eda-summaries-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Compute mean and median, then decide whether mean-only summarises the shape you need to see.

steps.label: Compute mean and median
steps.attempt_cue: Average the five counts; then take the middle ordered value.
steps.explanation: Ordered counts are 0, 0, 1, 3, 10. The mean is pulled by the large count; the median sits at the middle observation.

steps.label: Choose exploratory tools for shape
steps.attempt_cue: Name a plot/summary that shows zero mass and the right tail.
steps.explanation: A bar chart or histogram of counts (or a zero-aware frequency plot) reveals mass at zero and the long tail. Mean-only hides both features.
steps.calculation: Prefer histogram/bar (zero-aware) over mean-only; median/IQR support the centre/spread story

steps.label: Refuse pie / mean-only
steps.attempt_cue: State why a pie of policies or mean-only fails the exploratory aim.
steps.explanation: A pie chart of policies does not display the count distribution's zero inflation and tail. A mean of 2.8 alone misrepresents the typical frequency shape.
steps.calculation: Refuse pie-of-policies and mean-only as shape EDA
steps.result: Mean-only / pie rejected for this aim

cr-1.2.1-eda-summaries-cs1017.json.final_answer: Mean = 2.8 and median = 1; use a histogram or bar chart of counts (with median/IQR support) to reveal zero mass and the right tail. Refuse mean-only or a pie chart for this exploratory aim.
cr-1.2.1-eda-summaries-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Reporting only the mean count 2.8 as the exploratory summary, which hides zero-inflation and the long right tail that the modelling stage must confront.

cr-1.2.2-correlation-cs1017.json.title: Choose Spearman when association is monotone but skewed
cr-1.2.2-correlation-cs1017.json.problem_statement: For years licensed versus claim frequency, frequency is skewed with outliers and the scatter looks roughly decreasing but nonlinear. Software reports Pearson r = −0.28 and Spearman ρ = −0.55. Which correlation measure should you prefer for describing the association, and what must you still refuse?

given.value: roughly decreasing, nonlinear; skewed frequency with outliers

cr-1.2.2-correlation-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Match measure to linear vs monotone-nonlinear association, then separate association from causation.

steps.label: Match measure to association type
steps.attempt_cue: Say what Pearson vs Spearman each target.
steps.explanation: Pearson measures linear association. Spearman uses ranks and suits monotone but nonlinear patterns, with better resistance to outliers in many skewed cases.
steps.calculation: Pattern = monotone nonlinear + outliers → prefer Spearman (or Kendall)

steps.label: Read the two reported coefficients
steps.attempt_cue: Compare |r| and |ρ| in light of the scatter.
steps.explanation: The weaker Pearson value is expected when the relationship is not linear. The stronger Spearman value better reflects the monotone decrease under skew and outliers.
steps.calculation: |ρ| = 0.55 > |r| = 0.28; rank measure captures monotone association better here
steps.result: Report Spearman ρ = −0.55 as the preferred description

steps.label: Refuse causation from correlation
steps.attempt_cue: State what a large coefficient still does not prove.
steps.explanation: A large correlation coefficient does not prove that changing years licensed causes frequency to change.
steps.calculation: Association ≠ causation (even if |ρ| is large)
steps.result: Refuse causal claim from correlation alone

cr-1.2.2-correlation-cs1017.json.final_answer: Prefer Spearman ρ = −0.55 (monotone, skewed, outlier-prone) over Pearson r = −0.28. A large coefficient still does not prove causation.
cr-1.2.2-correlation-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Defaulting to Pearson because it is the familiar default, or treating Spearman ρ = −0.55 as proof that more years licensed causes lower claim frequency.

cr-1.2.3-pca-cs1017.json.title: Refuse treating PC1 as a causal auto-decline score
cr-1.2.3-pca-cs1017.json.problem_statement: A colleague says: 'PC1 from our rating factors is the true underlying risk score, so we can treat it as a causal driver and auto-decline on PC1 alone.' Decide what PCA actually provides here, and whether that auto-decline justification holds.

given.value: PC1 = true causal risk score; auto-decline on PC1 alone
dimensionality reduction on correlated rating factors

cr-1.2.3-pca-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Separate 'summarises shared variation' from 'proven causal driver' before judging the auto-decline claim.

steps.label: State what PCA constructs
steps.attempt_cue: Describe principal components in variation terms.
steps.explanation: PCA builds orthogonal components that capture major patterns of variation among correlated variables. A component is a weighted combination summarising shared variation.
steps.calculation: PC1 = leading variation summary (weighted combination), not a named causal mechanism by itself

steps.label: Separate summary from causation
steps.attempt_cue: Say whether PC1 proves a causal risk driver.
steps.explanation: Summarising shared variation does not by itself prove that PC1 is a causal risk driver. Causal claims need external subject-matter warrants beyond the eigenstructure.
steps.calculation: Variation summary ≠ proven causal driver
steps.result: Refuse causal identity for PC1 alone

steps.label: Judge the auto-decline proposal
steps.attempt_cue: Accept or refuse auto-decline on PC1 alone.
steps.explanation: Auto-decline on PC1 alone lacks decision and subject-matter warrants. PC1 may still be useful for exploration or visualisation of correlated rating factors.
steps.calculation: Judgment: REFUSE auto-decline-on-PC1-alone; allow exploratory use of PC1 as variation summary
steps.result: Refuse causal auto-decline; PC1 may still summarise variation

cr-1.2.3-pca-cs1017.json.final_answer: PC1 may summarise major shared variation among rating factors for exploration, but it does not by itself prove a causal risk driver or justify auto-decline without external warrants.
cr-1.2.3-pca-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Treating the first principal component as the 'true risk score' and using it as a standalone causal decline rule because it explains the most variance.

cr-2.1.1-discrete-cs1017.json.title: Select Poisson for rare annual claim counts
cr-2.1.1-discrete-cs1017.json.problem_statement: For a single policy, model the number of claims in a fixed year with a constant rare-event rate and independent increments. Choose the matching discrete family. As a light numeric check, if λ = 0.4 under that family, compute P(X = 0).

given.value: rare events in a fixed year; constant rate; independent increments

cr-2.1.1-discrete-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Match the generative story to a named discrete family before evaluating P(X = 0).

steps.label: Match story to family
steps.attempt_cue: Name the discrete family for rare events in a fixed interval under constant rate.
steps.explanation: Poisson counts rare events in a fixed interval under a constant rate / independent-increments story. Binomial needs a fixed number of independent trials; hypergeometric needs without-replacement draws from a finite population.
steps.calculation: Story → Poisson (not Normal; not hypergeometric)

steps.label: Light numeric illustration P(X = 0)
steps.attempt_cue: For Poisson(λ = 0.4), evaluate e^{−λ}.
steps.explanation: Under Poisson(λ), P(X = 0) = e^{−λ}. The numeric check confirms the chosen family is usable, not a substitute for the family-selection judgment.

steps.label: Refuse Normal / hypergeometric mismatch
steps.attempt_cue: State why Normal or hypergeometric fails this story.
steps.explanation: Normal has continuous all-real support and is a poor first match for a non-negative integer count. Hypergeometric requires a without-replacement finite success/failure population, which this policy-year rare-event story does not provide.
steps.calculation: Refuse Normal count model and hypergeometric without finite draw story

cr-2.1.1-discrete-cs1017.json.final_answer: Choose Poisson for the rare-event fixed-year count story; with λ = 0.4, P(X = 0) ≈ 0.6703. Refuse Normal or hypergeometric for this generative story.
cr-2.1.1-discrete-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Defaulting to a Normal model for claim counts because it is familiar, or picking hypergeometric without a without-replacement finite-population draw story.

cr-2.1.2-continuous-cs1017.json.title: Select Exponential for memoryless waiting times
cr-2.1.2-continuous-cs1017.json.problem_statement: Inter-claim waiting times are strictly positive and, under a constant hazard story, memoryless. Choose the matching continuous family. As a light numeric check, if the mean waiting time is 6 months, compute P(T > 6).

given.value: strictly positive waiting times; constant hazard; memoryless

cr-2.1.2-continuous-cs1017.json.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Match support and memorylessness to a named continuous family before evaluating the survival probability.

steps.label: Match story to family
steps.attempt_cue: Name the continuous family for positive memoryless waiting times.
steps.explanation: Exponential models positive memoryless waiting times under constant hazard. Normal has symmetric all-real support and is a poor default for strictly positive waits.
steps.calculation: Story → Exponential (refuse Normal-by-default)

steps.label: Light numeric illustration P(T > 6)
steps.attempt_cue: For Exponential mean 6, evaluate the survival at t = 6.
steps.explanation: With mean θ = 6, P(T > t) = e^{−t/θ}. At the mean, survival equals e^{−1}. The numeric check illustrates the chosen family; family selection remains the LO hinge.

steps.label: Refuse Normal-by-default
steps.attempt_cue: State the support mismatch for a Normal waiting-time model.
steps.explanation: A Normal model allows negative waiting times and is not memoryless. That mismatches the stated positive constant-hazard story.
steps.calculation: Normal support includes negatives; not memoryless → refuse

cr-2.1.2-continuous-cs1017.json.final_answer: Choose Exponential for positive memoryless waiting times; with mean 6 months, P(T > 6) ≈ 0.3679. Refuse Normal-by-default for this story.
cr-2.1.2-continuous-cs1017.json.common_pitfall: Defaulting to a Normal waiting-time model because it is familiar, ignoring that waiting times are strictly positive and memoryless under constant hazard.
